title: Autoimmune beta-cell loss
summary: In T1D the immune system damages insulin-producing beta cells in pancreatic islets.
why: This explains why a person may need insulin even when they eat well and exercise.
how: Loss of functioning beta cells reduces the body’s ability to match insulin release to changes in blood glucose.
example: A learner compares autoimmunity with a lock-and-key picture of insulin resistance and asks how the two differ.
caution: Autoimmunity cannot be diagnosed from a glucose trace alone.
question: Is T1D caused by eating too much sugar?
answer: No. Its defining process is autoimmune beta-cell damage.

title: Pancreatic alpha and beta cells
summary: Alpha cells produce glucagon; beta cells make insulin. Both belong to pancreatic islets.
why: Understanding their different roles helps explain background glucose regulation and low-glucose rescue.
how: Insulin supports glucose use and storage. Glucagon signals the liver to release glucose when fuel is needed.
example: During a lesson someone maps the two hormones to the organs that make and respond to them.
caution: The body’s response to hypoglycemia in T1D may be impaired. Physiology diagrams cannot predict an individual response.
question: Which cells make insulin?
answer: Beta cells. Alpha cells have a different role.
takeaways: Alpha and beta cells have different roles

title: C-peptide
summary: C-peptide is released when the body makes its own insulin from a precursor molecule.
why: Measuring it can help a clinician assess remaining insulin production.
how: Injected insulin does not contain C-peptide. Interpretation depends on timing, glucose at testing and clinical circumstances.
example: An adult asks why the clinician requested a glucose measurement alongside C-peptide.
caution: A single result cannot determine a treatment change or diabetes type in isolation.
question: Does injected insulin directly raise C-peptide?
answer: No. C-peptide comes from endogenous insulin production.

title: Islet autoantibodies
summary: GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8 and insulin autoantibodies are markers associated with an autoimmune response affecting islets.
why: They can help classification and identify people who may need specialist follow-up before symptoms.
how: Clinicians consider which antibodies are present, whether findings persist and the person’s glucose status.
example: A relative with a positive screen asks about confirmation and follow-up rather than assuming clinical diabetes.
caution: An antibody result alone does not establish a personal timeline or a need for insulin today.
question: Do autoantibodies measure glucose?
answer: No. They answer an immune-system question.

title: Insulin resistance in T1D
summary: A person with autoimmune insulin deficiency can also have reduced sensitivity to insulin.
why: Illness, puberty and other changes may alter requirements without changing the T1D diagnosis.
how: Muscle, liver and fat may respond less strongly to the available insulin. Absorption or delivery problems can mimic a change in sensitivity.
example: During an illness a clinician reviews delivery and injection sites alongside the glucose record.
caution: Do not diagnose resistance from dose size alone. Check possible delivery problems and illness with the team.
question: Does insulin resistance automatically turn T1D into type 2?
answer: No. Different physiological processes can coexist.

title: Immunotherapy and disease modification
summary: Immune therapies aim to alter the autoimmune process at defined stages of T1D.
why: Approval for one disease stage, age or country does not imply approval for every person with T1D.
how: US evidence snapshot, June 2026: the FDA label for teplizumab includes delaying stage 3 onset in eligible people aged one year and older with stage 2 T1D. A separate accelerated indication addresses decline in endogenous insulin production in eligible recently diagnosed children aged 8–17.
example: A family takes an antibody result to a specialist to discuss staging and eligibility under local rules.
caution: The US label includes serious viral reactivation warnings and clinical monitoring requirements. This is specialist treatment, not an insulin substitute.
question: Does a US approval establish availability in India?
answer: No. Local approval, eligibility and access must be checked independently.

title: Islet cell transplantation
summary: Donor islet transplantation transfers insulin-producing islets from a deceased donor into a recipient.
why: It is an option for a narrowly defined group, with substantial risks and long-term follow-up.
how: US FDA approval in 2023 covered donislecel for selected adults with T1D and repeated severe hypoglycemia despite intensive management. Maintaining donor cells generally requires immunosuppression.
example: A reader checks the indication and risks in the FDA label after seeing a transplant headline.
caution: Insulin independence is not guaranteed. Immunosuppression can increase infection and other risks.
question: Are donor islets and stem-cell-derived islets the same product?
answer: No. They differ in cell source, evidence and regulatory status.

title: Stem-cell-derived islet research
summary: Researchers can grow insulin-producing islet-like cells from stem cells for study as a replacement therapy.
why: A renewable source of cells could address some limitations of donor supply.
how: A 2025 early-phase study of zimislecel assessed transplanted cells in people with T1D receiving immunosuppression. It provided evidence of function in a selected trial population.
example: A reader checks participant numbers, follow-up duration and whether immunosuppression was required before interpreting a headline.
caution: This is a dated research example. A trial result alone does not establish routine approval, long-term safety or local access.
question: What evidence would strengthen an early result?
answer: Larger studies, longer follow-up, safety data and regulatory assessment.

title: Artificial pancreas systems
summary: An artificial pancreas system links sensing, decision software and insulin delivery in a feedback loop.
why: It illustrates both the possibilities and limits of replacing a biological control system.
how: The algorithm reacts to estimated glucose changes, while insulin absorption and sensor lag introduce delays. User tasks depend on the device.
example: A learner draws three arrows between the CGM, controller and pump and identifies where a lost signal matters.
caution: Marketing terms do not specify compatibility or how much meal input is needed. Read the actual device instructions.
question: Does “closed loop” mean no human input?
answer: Many systems are hybrid and still require meal announcements and maintenance.

title: Emerging CGM and insulin technology
summary: New devices and formulations are evaluated for accuracy, usability, safety and clinical outcomes.
why: A promising prototype, a cleared product and a locally supported product are different milestones.
how: Technology studies specify a population, comparator and outcome. Accuracy under study conditions is only one part of real-world use.
example: A reader compares a research announcement with the manufacturer’s current instructions in their country.
caution: Check the evidence date, approval region, device version and whether the claim comes from a trial or an advertisement.
question: Does a new feature work with every phone or pump?
answer: Compatibility is specific to a model and software version.

title: Prevention and screening research
summary: Screening can identify markers of early autoimmune T1D before clinical symptoms appear.
why: Follow-up can support education and timely recognition of progression.
how: Staging combines immune markers and glucose findings. Some studies recruit only people at a particular stage or level of risk.
example: A relative considering screening asks what follow-up is available after each possible result.
caution: A negative screen is not a lifetime guarantee. Research participation and approved treatment have different eligibility rules.
question: Is screening itself a preventive treatment?
answer: No. It identifies risk or disease stage and may guide follow-up.

title: Type 1, type 2 and other diabetes types
summary: Diabetes can result from different mechanisms, including autoimmune insulin deficiency, insulin resistance, genetic changes or pancreatic disease.
why: Classification can affect treatment and whether relatives should be offered testing.
how: History, examination and selected laboratory tests help distinguish aetiologies. Symptoms and body size overlap.
example: A newly diagnosed adult asks what supports the proposed type and what would prompt reassessment.
caution: Never stop insulin while seeking a second opinion about classification.
question: Can a single glucose measurement show diabetes type?
answer: No. It measures glucose, not the cause.
